The central idea

The extension controls the convergence

The even extension joins continuously at ±π, although its slope changes there. Its cosine coefficients fall roughly as 1/n². The odd extension creates a jump at the period boundary, so its sine coefficients fall more slowly and produce Gibbs oscillations.

Cosineaₙ = 4(−1)ⁿ / n²
Sinebₙ has a leading 1/n term

Cosine converges faster for this extension

Why the sine endpoint never matches: every term contains sin(nπ), which is zero. Therefore the sine partial sum equals zero at x = π while the target value is π².

Heat conduction lab

Watch Fourier modes fade with time

A one-dimensional model shows how a central hot region spreads through an 80 cm surface.

Peak temperature 180.0°C Boundary model Sine · fixed temperature

Cooled ends

The temperature difference from the room vanishes at both ends. Sine modes satisfy those boundary values automatically.

Insulated ends

No heat crosses the ends, so the temperature gradient is zero there. Cosine modes satisfy that condition.

Educational model: heat flows in one dimension, material properties are representative, and air convection is omitted.

Daily-life scenario

A hot pan on a kitchen countertop

Move the pan, choose the countertop, and see how the same Fourier logic predicts the spreading warmth.

What you feel

Warmth spreads away from the pan

Material near the pan heats first. With time, the hottest region falls and the warm region widens.

What the mathematics sees

Many modes become a temperature profile

High-frequency modes describe sharp changes and fade quickly. Lower modes remain longer, making the profile smoother.
